newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada GDP rises, current account in surplus.
newsitem.headline: Canada GDP rises, current account in surplus.

text.p: Canada's economy grew at the fastest rate in nearly two years in the third quarter, the government said Friday, aided by sharp declines in Canadian interest rates this year.
Statistics Canada said gross domestic product grew by a seasonally adjusted 0.8 percent in the third quarter from the second quarter, for an annualized growth rate of 3.3 percent.
A Reuters survey of economists had forecast a 0.7 percent rise after a 0.3 percent increase in the second quarter.

The government agency said the third-quarter growth rate -- the biggest quarterly gain since the fourth quarter of 1994 -- was fuelled by merchandise exports, residential construction and a farm inventory build-up.

The agency also said Canada posted its second straight current account surplus in the quarter, though it fell to C$551 million ($409.5 million) from C$1.09 billion ($810 million) in the second quarter.
Analysts said the report was evidence that aggressive rate-cutting by the central bank, the Bank of Canada, was working its way into the economy and that growth would accelerate.
"The low rate environment is definitely paying off," said John Anania, an economist with Royal Bank of Canada. "Going forward, it justifies looking at strong growth into 1997."

Canadian Finance Minister Paul Martin told reporters that the data showed that Canada's economy was "well-anchored" and he predicted that Canada's 10 percent unemployment rate would return to single-digit levels.
"What I see here is a progressive improvement in the economy," said Mark Mullins, chief economist with Midland Walwyn Capital Inc. "At a mimimum, we'll have quite strong numbers into the summertime."
The Bank of Canada has cut rates 11 times this year, bringing prime lending rates at major commercial banks to 4.75 percent, their lowest level in 40 years.
The growing strength of the economy suggested the Bank of Canada was unlikely to lower rates again in the near term, if at all, economists said.
In its most recent monetary policy report, the central bank said it would closely monitor growth.
Economists said the latest report confirmed the pickup and reduced the need for another rate cut.
"You can't really rule out another bank rate cut, but right now it's unlikely," said Royal Bank's Anania.
Economists said the only negative news in the reports was that consumer demand remained weak. Consumer confidence has remained low in Canada amid high unemployment and deficit cutting by governments.
"The consumer was still very close to dead in the water," said Randall Powley, senior economist with Scotia Capital Markets.
